speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) how many self-driving vehicles are currently being test-driven on our public roads; and (b) what safety measures are in place to ensure the safety of pedestrians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Further trials in more complex environments will be allowed when AVs are able to demonstrate a higher level of competence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: All AVs must have a vehicle fault alert system that will alert the safety driver of any faults, and allow the control of the vehicle to be immediately transferred to the safety driver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We are mindful that AV technology is evolving rapidly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will review these measures regularly and enhance them if necessary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my work with the National Transport Workers' Union, they are very concerned with the deployment of AVs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I visit quite a number of companies which are experimenting with AVs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yes, they all tell me their primary priority is safety of their vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Earlier this year, a self-driving Uber car killed a woman on a street in Arizona, USA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: News reports stated that the car was in autonomous mode and there was a legal operator inside the car at the time of the accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This threw in doubt the safety measures that most companies have already put into the development of the car.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given that we have plans to roll out self-driving vehicles, buses, on our public roads in the near future, how can we determine whether a particular self-driving vehicle model is safe before we put it onto the road?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would LTA consider delaying deploying such self-driving vehicles until we are fully assured of the safety of all our road users?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As far as the first question on how we can be sure that a vehicle is safe, in my answer to the Parliamentary Question (PQ), I have listed the many steps and considerations that we are taking: a given technology, a given process and a specific entity, organisation or company, from a limited road trial to an extended road trial and a complex environment road trial.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We must also consider what it is that we are comparing them against.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Absolute safety is very hard to determine in any situation or any technology.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the reality is that human-piloted vehicles are not absolutely safe and we do see a significant number of accidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the key concerns about how we develop AVs is to make sure that our roads, over time, become safer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is not just about making sure it becomes as safe as today, but safer than today, and that is the destination we wish to go to.
